screens.title: Selecting metrics with metric names
screens.narratorSegment: Start with the simplest PromQL query: the metric name itself. When you type a metric such as node_cpu_seconds_total into Prometheus it returns an instant vector containing every series with that metric name. Each series differs by labels — for example instance, C P U, and mode — which are dimensions you can later filter or aggregate. Selecting a metric without labels is useful for exploration but often too noisy for dashboards; you will usually add label matchers to focus on a subset. A concrete example is node_cpu_seconds_total which includes different modes like idle and user. Typing the bare name helps you discover which labels exist in your environment. A common misconception is thinking a metric name returns a single number; in reality it returns multiple series, one per label combination. To confirm what you received, check the label set shown in the Graph tab and note which labels vary. Closing question: after typing a metric, what labels matter for your dashboard — instance, mode, or C P U — and which should you aggregate away? Selecting metrics with metric names means a metric name returns multiple series distinguished by labels; use selection to discover available dimensions.. In practical terms, how raw metric names return sets of series you can work with. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Metric selection
Definition
A raw metric name selects all series with that name, each identified by labels.
Why it matters

Discovering the full label set for a metric lets you decide how to filter and aggregate. Use the raw name when exploring what dimensions are available in your environment.

Common misconception

A metric name does not return a single number; it returns a set of series, one per label combination.

Key Takeaway

Start with the bare metric to discover labels, then refine with matchers or aggregations for dashboards.

Concrete example
node_cpu_seconds_total

Execute this in Graph to see many series. Look for labels such as instance, cpu, and mode to guide your next filter.

Try this

After running the bare metric, note which label varies most and plan whether to preserve it with by() or drop it with without().

screens.title: Label matchers and operators
screens.narratorSegment: Label matchers let you narrow which time series a selector returns. Labels are key-value pairs attached to every series, and they are case-sensitive. PromQL supports four main matchers: equals, not-equals, regex match, and negative-regex match. For example, node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"} returns series where the mode label equals idle. To exclude a mode, use mode!="idle". Regex matchers let you match multiple values at once, for example mode=~"idle|user". Regex not match lets you exclude groups of values. A common mistake is assuming matchers are case-insensitive or that partial text matches without regex; both are false. Use matchers to reduce noise before aggregating. Concrete example: node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="idle", C P U="0"} filters out idle modes and selects a specific C P U core, which is useful when computing per-core or per-instance aggregates. Closing question: which matcher would you use to select both idle and user modes but exclude system? Label matchers and operators means use =, !=, =~, and !~ to precisely include or exclude series based on label values.. In practical terms, filter time series with exact and regex label matchers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Label matching
keyIdea.text: Use =, !=, =~, and !~ to precisely include or exclude series based on label values.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Label matchers
Matcher quick reference
  • = exact equals, for example mode="idle"
  • != not equals, for example mode!="idle"
  • =~ regex match, for example mode=~"idle|user"
  • !~ regex negative match, for example mode!~"idle|user"
Why this matters

Match only the series you need before applying functions or aggregation. This keeps graphs readable and alerts accurate.

Common mistake

Assuming matchers are case-insensitive or that regex is implied. Explicitly use =~ for regex and respect case.

Concrete examples
node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}
node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="idle", cpu="0"}
node_cpu_seconds_total{mode=~"idle|user"}

Try these in Graph to see how the returned series change. Notice label lists for each series so you can plan aggregation.

screens.title: Instant vectors vs Range vectors
screens.narratorSegment: A critical concept in PromQL is the difference between instant and range vectors. An instant vector is a set of series each with a single sample at one timestamp. It’s the result you get when you query the Graph for a single point in time. A range vector is a set of series where each series has multiple samples across a specified time window; you create one by appending a duration in square brackets, like five minutes. Range vectors are the only valid inputs for many functions that compute change over time, such as rate or delta. For example, rate(metric[5m]) needs the last five minutes of samples to calculate an average per-second increase. A common misconception is trying to feed instant-only math functions results that actually need a range; this will either be invalid or produce meaningless output. Concrete example: node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m] produces a range vector you can summarize with rate. Closing question: if you want a smoothed per-second rate that averages short spikes, would you increase or decrease the range window, and why? Instant vectors vs Range vectors means instant vectors are single-sample series; range vectors include multiple samples over a duration and are required by many functions.. In practical terms, when to use a single sample versus a historical window. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Vectors explained
keyIdea.text: Instant vectors are single-sample series; range vectors include multiple samples over a duration and are required by many functions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Vectors
Definition & use

Use instant vectors when you need the current snapshot across series. Use range vectors when a function must inspect historical samples to compute rates or deltas.

Example
node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}          # instant vector
node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m]       # range vector for last 5 minutes
rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])  # valid use of range vector
Misconception

Trying to call rate() without a range or feeding an instant vector to functions expecting ranges will produce errors or meaningless results. Always check function requirements.

Practical tip

Short windows like one minute reveal bursts but are noisy; longer windows smooth spikes but can hide short incidents. Choose the window to match the signal you want to highlight.

Key Takeaway

Range vectors provide history needed by functions; instant vectors give a snapshot. Match the vector type to the function's needs.

screens.title: Using rate() and irate() on counters
screens.narratorSegment: Counters are metrics that only increase, like the total number of HTTP requests. Their raw values are rarely useful to display directly because they always climb. The rate function computes the average per-second increase over a given range, which is usually what you want on dashboards. For example, rate(http_requests_total[10m]) returns requests per second averaged over ten minutes. irate computes the instantaneous rate using the two most recent samples, which can reveal sudden bursts but is noisier. A concrete example is comparing rate and irate on a network counter: use rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total[5m]) for steady bandwidth and irate for short spikes during a file transfer. A common mistake is applying rate to a gauge; gauges measure current state and can go up and down, so rate will produce misleading results. To practice, select a known counter and run both rate and irate with different windows and observe smoothing versus responsiveness. Closing question: when would you prefer irate over rate and why might that matter for alerting? Using rate() and irate() on counters means use rate to compute averaged per-second increases from counters; use irate for instant, burst-sensitive values.. In practical terms, turn monotonically increasing counters into per-second rates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use rate to compute averaged per-second increases from counters; use irate for instant, burst-sensitive values.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Rate & irate
What rate() does

rate(metric[duration]) computes the average per-second increase of a counter over the specified window. It smooths spikes and reduces noise from sampling variability.

What irate() does

irate uses the two most recent samples to estimate an instantaneous per-second rate. It is more responsive but noisier.

Common mistake

Applying rate() to a gauge will give nonsensical results because gauges can decrease. Only use rate on counters.

Examples to run
rate(http_requests_total[10m])
irate(http_requests_total[1m])
rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total[5m])

Try these with different windows to see how smoothing changes. Use rate for dashboarding and irate for short anomaly detection when you want immediate changes reflected.

Pro tip

For alerting, prefer a slightly longer rate window to avoid firing on brief, harmless spikes unless the alert specifically requires instant response.

screens.title: Arithmetic operations on vectors
screens.narratorSegment: PromQL supports arithmetic directly on instant vectors, letting you build derived metrics like percentages or per-core values. Operators include addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. A common pattern is converting C P U seconds into a percentage. For example, you might compute 100 minus the average idle rate multiplied by 100 to get non-idle C P U percentage. When doing arithmetic across vectors, pay attention to matching label sets. Prometheus will perform vector matching automatically when series share identical labels, but mismatched labels can cause unexpected series to be dropped or scalar values to be applied. A concrete example from the chapter computes non-idle C P U percent as 100 - (avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100). A typical misconception is forgetting to aggregate before arithmetic, which can lead to per-series math when you wanted an aggregated result. Closing question: when dividing two vectors where labels differ, how would you ensure the division groups by instance? Arithmetic operations on vectors means use +, -, *, and / on vectors to compute derived metrics, and ensure label sets align or aggregate appropriately.. In practical terms, compute percentages, ratios, and derived metrics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Arithmetic
When to use arithmetic

Create percentages, normalize metrics across instances, or combine counters into totals. Always consider label alignment first.

Label matching caution

If two vectors have different label sets, the arithmetic may not match series as you expect. Use aggregation by() to align labels before arithmetic if needed.

Key Takeaway

Aggregate or align labels before arithmetic to ensure results represent the intended grouping.

Concrete example
100 - (avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100)

This computes non-idle CPU percentage per instance by averaging the idle rate and converting to percent, then subtracting from 100.

screens.title: Aggregation operators: sum, avg, count
screens.narratorSegment: Aggregation operators let you collapse many series into summaries. sum(), avg(), count(), min(), and max() are commonly used to produce totals, averages, and counts across dimensions. By default an aggregation collapses all labels and returns a single result per metric. To preserve useful dimensions, use by() to specify which labels to keep, and without() to drop labels. For example, sum(node_cpu_seconds_total) by (mode) returns a total per C P U mode across all instances. If you want to average memory across hosts but ignore the instance label, use avg(node_memory_MemFree_bytes) without (instance). A common error is forgetting by() or without(), which can unexpectedly reduce your series to a single scalar. Practical example: sum(rate(http_requests_total[10m])) by (service) gives total requests per second per service. When designing dashboards, think about which labels you need to see and which you need to remove to avoid data explosion. Closing question: when would you choose without(instance) versus by(instance)? Aggregation operators: sum, avg, count means use aggregation operators with by() or without() to control which label dimensions are preserved in the output.. In practical terms, summarize series and control dimensions with by() and without(). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

If you want to average memory across hosts but ignore the instance label, use avg(node_memory_MemFree_bytes) without (instance). content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Aggregation
How aggregation works

Aggregation combines multiple series into a smaller set by applying a function across matching series. Use by() to keep labels you care about or without() to drop noisy labels.

Examples
sum(node_cpu_seconds_total) by (mode)
avg(node_memory_MemFree_bytes) without (instance)
sum(rate(http_requests_total[10m])) by (service)
Common mistake

Forgetting by() can collapse data into a single scalar, hiding per-instance or per-service variation that is important for troubleshooting.

Quick decision guide
  • Keep labels with by() when you need per-group metrics.
  • Use without() to remove labels that cause unnecessary series count.
  • Combine aggregation with rate for per-second group metrics.
Key Takeaway

Plan aggregations by deciding which labels must remain for meaningful dashboards and alerts.

screens.title: Network I/O and combining counters
screens.narratorSegment: Network telemetry is a common use case for rate functions. Network counters record cumulative bytes transmitted or received, so converting them to bytes per second is essential. Use rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total[1m]) to compute recent receive bandwidth in bytes per second. screens.title: Pitfalls and debugging PromQL
screens.narratorSegment: When learning PromQL you'll run into a few recurring mistakes. First, applying rate() to a gauge is a frequent error; gauges can go up and down, so rate produces meaningless trends. Second, label matching is case-sensitive; mistyping a label value will silently return no series. Third, aggregation without by() will collapse series into a single value, often hiding important per-instance or per-service variation. Fourth, vector mismatches during arithmetic can drop series when labels differ. To debug, start by running the raw selector to inspect labels, then gradually add matchers, range durations, and functions. Use small windows and compare rate versus irate to understand smoothing. A useful troubleshooting step is to explicitly list labels in by() to ensure the grouping matches your intent. Closing question: when you see fewer series than expected after an arithmetic operation, what sequence of checks would you run to find the cause? screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the core concepts to remember as you practice. PromQL selects and transforms time series: a metric name returns series that are distinguished by labels. Label matchers allow precise filtering using equals, not-equals, regex, and negative-regex. Instant vectors are snapshots at a single timestamp, while range vectors include historical samples over a duration and are required for functions like rate. Aggregation operators such as sum and avg collapse series; use by or without to control preserved labels. Rate and irate turn counter deltas into per-second values: rate smooths over a window and irate is instantaneous and responsive. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we begin working with PromQL so you can ask precise questions of your telemetry. PromQL is the language Prometheus uses to pick time series, refine them with label matchers, apply functions, and produce numbers you can chart or alert on. We will start with the simplest queries — a single metric name — and then build up filters using labels, learn the difference between instant and range vectors, and practice transformations like arithmetic and aggregation. You will also see how rate functions turn raw counters into useful per-second values. For example, instead of plotting a monotonically increasing HTTP request counter, you will compute requests per second with rate(). That change in perspective is essential for interpreting activity. Along the way I’ll point out common mistakes, like using rate() on a gauge or forgetting to group by the correct label. By the end you’ll be able to write queries for C P U, memory, and network metrics and experiment confidently in the Prometheus Graph. Keep an eye out for short, hands-on examples you can paste directly into the Graph tab to see these ideas in action.

These objectives give you a clear path from selecting raw metrics to producing dashboard-ready series. First, you'll learn the syntax for selecting time series with metric names and label matchers so you can target the data you care about. Second, you'll understand the difference between instant vectors and range vectors; this distinction determines when to use functions like rate() that require historical samples. Third, you will practice arithmetic and comparison operators so you can compute percentages or compare series. Fourth, you'll master basic aggregation operators and use by and without clauses to control dimensions. Finally, you'll learn when and how to use rate() and irate() to convert counters into meaningful per-second rates. Each objective is paired with a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding with a short query in the Prometheus Graph tab. These skills are practical: they let you transform raw telemetry into metrics suitable for dashboards and alerts. As you work through the lessons, try the small examples to reach each milestone and see immediate results.

This second objectives slide maps each learning outcome to a short, practical verification you can perform. For metric selection, try typing a metric like node_cpu_seconds_total and then add a label matcher such as mode="idle" to see the filtered series. For vectors, execute a query that returns an instant vector, then add a range selector like open square bracket five minutes close bracket to return a range vector and feed it to a function. For arithmetic, compute a percentage by dividing two metrics and multiplying by 100, observing how the values change when labels differ. For aggregation, run sum by instance on a C P U metric and then run the same without instance to see the difference; that demonstrates grouping behavior. Finally, for rates, use rate(http_requests_total[10m]) and compare it with irate on a short window to see when each is appropriate. Each verification is intentionally small and repeatable in the Prometheus Graph, so you can reach competency quickly and iterate until the results match your expectations.

Start with the simplest PromQL query: the metric name itself. When you type a metric such as node_cpu_seconds_total into Prometheus it returns an instant vector containing every series with that metric name. Each series differs by labels — for example instance, C P U, and mode — which are dimensions you can later filter or aggregate. Selecting a metric without labels is useful for exploration but often too noisy for dashboards; you will usually add label matchers to focus on a subset. A concrete example is node_cpu_seconds_total which includes different modes like idle and user. Typing the bare name helps you discover which labels exist in your environment. A common misconception is thinking a metric name returns a single number; in reality it returns multiple series, one per label combination. To confirm what you received, check the label set shown in the Graph tab and note which labels vary. Closing question: after typing a metric, what labels matter for your dashboard — instance, mode, or C P U — and which should you aggregate away? Selecting metrics with metric names means a metric name returns multiple series distinguished by labels; use selection to discover available dimensions.. In practical terms, how raw metric names return sets of series you can work with. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Label matchers let you narrow which time series a selector returns. Labels are key-value pairs attached to every series, and they are case-sensitive. PromQL supports four main matchers: equals, not-equals, regex match, and negative-regex match. For example, node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"} returns series where the mode label equals idle. To exclude a mode, use mode!="idle". Regex matchers let you match multiple values at once, for example mode=~"idle|user". Regex not match lets you exclude groups of values. A common mistake is assuming matchers are case-insensitive or that partial text matches without regex; both are false. Use matchers to reduce noise before aggregating. Concrete example: node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="idle", C P U="0"} filters out idle modes and selects a specific C P U core, which is useful when computing per-core or per-instance aggregates. Closing question: which matcher would you use to select both idle and user modes but exclude system? Label matchers and operators means use =, !=, =~, and !~ to precisely include or exclude series based on label values.. In practical terms, filter time series with exact and regex label matchers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A critical concept in PromQL is the difference between instant and range vectors. An instant vector is a set of series each with a single sample at one timestamp. It’s the result you get when you query the Graph for a single point in time. A range vector is a set of series where each series has multiple samples across a specified time window; you create one by appending a duration in square brackets, like five minutes. Range vectors are the only valid inputs for many functions that compute change over time, such as rate or delta. For example, rate(metric[5m]) needs the last five minutes of samples to calculate an average per-second increase. A common misconception is trying to feed instant-only math functions results that actually need a range; this will either be invalid or produce meaningless output. Concrete example: node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m] produces a range vector you can summarize with rate. Closing question: if you want a smoothed per-second rate that averages short spikes, would you increase or decrease the range window, and why? Instant vectors vs Range vectors means instant vectors are single-sample series; range vectors include multiple samples over a duration and are required by many functions.. In practical terms, when to use a single sample versus a historical window. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Counters are metrics that only increase, like the total number of HTTP requests. Their raw values are rarely useful to display directly because they always climb. The rate function computes the average per-second increase over a given range, which is usually what you want on dashboards. For example, rate(http_requests_total[10m]) returns requests per second averaged over ten minutes. irate computes the instantaneous rate using the two most recent samples, which can reveal sudden bursts but is noisier. A concrete example is comparing rate and irate on a network counter: use rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total[5m]) for steady bandwidth and irate for short spikes during a file transfer. A common mistake is applying rate to a gauge; gauges measure current state and can go up and down, so rate will produce misleading results. To practice, select a known counter and run both rate and irate with different windows and observe smoothing versus responsiveness. Closing question: when would you prefer irate over rate and why might that matter for alerting? Using rate() and irate() on counters means use rate to compute averaged per-second increases from counters; use irate for instant, burst-sensitive values.. In practical terms, turn monotonically increasing counters into per-second rates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

PromQL supports arithmetic directly on instant vectors, letting you build derived metrics like percentages or per-core values. Operators include addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. A common pattern is converting C P U seconds into a percentage. For example, you might compute 100 minus the average idle rate multiplied by 100 to get non-idle C P U percentage. When doing arithmetic across vectors, pay attention to matching label sets. Prometheus will perform vector matching automatically when series share identical labels, but mismatched labels can cause unexpected series to be dropped or scalar values to be applied. A concrete example from the chapter computes non-idle C P U percent as 100 - (avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100). Let's summarize the core concepts to remember as you practice. PromQL selects and transforms time series: a metric name returns series that are distinguished by labels. Label matchers allow precise filtering using equals, not-equals, regex, and negative-regex. Instant vectors are snapshots at a single timestamp, while range vectors include historical samples over a duration and are required for functions like rate. Aggregation operators such as sum and avg collapse series; use by or without to control preserved labels. Rate and irate turn counter deltas into per-second values: rate smooths over a window and irate is instantaneous and responsive. Common mistakes include using rate on gauges, mismatched labels during arithmetic, and forgetting to group before aggregating.
